---
title: "Flag conditions"
description: >
  Turn reviewed lists of diagnosis codes into TRUE, FALSE or NA for each entry,
  and flag diabetes on the entry admission or in the year before.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Print results at most 60 characters wide, "#> " included, to fit a printed page.
options(width = 57)
# Keep the build machine out of printed query headers (load duckdb first, as it
# registers its own description when it loads).
loadNamespace("duckdb")
registerS3method("db_connection_describe", "duckdb_connection",
                 function(con, ...) "example database", envir = asNamespace("dbplyr"))
```

The running question compares people with and without diabetes. Diabetes can
be recorded on the entry admission, whose codes are in `candidates`, or on the
admissions in the year before, which [Look back and follow
up](look-back-follow-up.html) fetched into `history`. This guide turns those
records into one answer per entry.

A condition, in this course, is a list of codes you have reviewed. `icd_flag()`
takes records and one or more lists, and gives one row per ID with a column of
`TRUE`, `FALSE` or `NA` for each list:

```{r condition-flags, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Inline, so the diagram travels with the page and keeps its title and description.
cat("```{=html}", "<div style=\"margin: 0.5rem 0 1.5rem;\">",
    readLines("figures/condition-flags.svg"), "</div>", "```", sep = "\n")
```

Every example runs on the example database of invented records described in
[Meet the THIP data](meet-the-data.html); on THIP, connect with `thip_connect()`
instead.

## Rebuild the entries and history

This chunk repeats earlier guides: the recipe of [From question to
cohort](question-to-cohort.html), then the `history` call of [Look back and
follow up](look-back-follow-up.html).

```{r rebuild}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- thip_connect_example()

admissions <- thip_table(
  con,
  tables = c("nhso2565", "nhso2566", "nhso2567"),
  .id = "source_table",
  dates = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc"),
  date_format = c(adm = "%Y%m%d", dsc = "%Y%m%d")
)

candidates <- admissions |>
  filter(adm >= as.Date("2021-10-01"),
         adm <= as.Date("2024-08-31")) |>
  thip_filter_icd(codes = "K35", cols = "pdx",
                  match = "prefix") |>
  collect()

entries <- candidates |>
  filter(!is.na(dsc)) |>
  arrange(pid, adm, tran_id) |>
  distinct(pid, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(pid, entry_id = tran_id,
         adm_date = adm, dsc_date = dsc)

history <- admissions |>
  select(pid, tran_id, source_table, adm, dsc, pdx,
         num_range("sdx", 1:20)) |>
  thip_window(entries, date = "adm", index = "adm_date",
              window = c(-365L, 0L)) |>
  collect()

c(entries = nrow(entries), history = nrow(history))
```

There are `r nrow(entries)` entries, and `history` holds `r nrow(history)`
records from the year before them.

## Flag diabetes in each period

In this course, an entry has diabetes when a code starting E10 to E14 appears
in any diagnosis position on the entry admission or in the year before it.
Write the codes as a named list, whose name becomes the column of answers. The
lists in this guide illustrate the method and are not validated definitions:
review your own, and report them with your methods.

The entry admission is in `candidates`, under its `tran_id`. Keep the
candidates that became entries, rename `tran_id` to `entry_id` so that both
periods share one ID, and flag each period in `pdx` and `sdx1` to `sdx20`:

```{r flag}
dm <- list(diabetes = paste0("E", 10:14))
dx_cols <- c("pdx", paste0("sdx", 1:20))

entry_admissions <- candidates |>
  filter(tran_id %in% entries$entry_id) |>
  rename(entry_id = tran_id)

on_entry <- icd_flag(entry_admissions, dm, id = "entry_id",
                     cols = dx_cols, match = "prefix")
in_history <- icd_flag(history, dm, id = "entry_id",
                       cols = dx_cols, match = "prefix")

glimpse(on_entry)
glimpse(in_history)
```

`id` names the column to answer for: `icd_flag()` combines every record with
the same ID, across rows and the columns in `cols`, into one row of a new table;
join it back to see other columns. `match = "prefix"` matches every code that
starts with one on the list ([Exact or prefix](#exact-or-prefix); every
argument is on [the reference page](../reference/icd_flag.html)).

`in_history` has only `r nrow(in_history)` rows: an entry with no records in the
year before gets no row. `icd_flag()` reads no dates, so the window you fetched
decides which records count. `id = "pid"` would pool all of a person's records,
so keep `entry_id` when a person can have several entries.

## TRUE, FALSE and NA

Each answer takes one of three values:

- `TRUE`: at least one selected code is on the list.
- `FALSE`: codes were recorded, but none is on the list. No diabetes code was
  recorded; that is not proof that the person has no diabetes.
- `NA`: no code was recorded in that period. `icd_flag()` gives `NA` when every
  selected column of an ID's records is blank or missing; an entry with no
  records has no row, so it gets `NA` when you join.

To keep every entry, start from `entries` and left-join both results; `suffix`
names the two `diabetes` columns by period:

```{r by-period}
by_period <- entries |>
  select(entry_id) |>
  left_join(on_entry, by = "entry_id") |>
  left_join(in_history, by = "entry_id",
            suffix = c("_entry", "_history"))

count(by_period, diabetes_entry, diabetes_history)
```

Every entry admission has codes, so `diabetes_entry` is never `NA`; it is `TRUE`
for `r sum(on_entry$diabetes)` entries. `diabetes_history` is `NA` for the
`r sum(is.na(by_period$diabetes_history))` entries with no records in the year
before.

## Combine the periods

This course counts an entry as having diabetes when either period has a code,
and reads `NA` as "no diabetes code recorded", the same as `FALSE`. In R,
`FALSE | NA` is `NA`, so `coalesce()` turns `NA` into `FALSE` first:

```{r combine}
flags <- by_period |>
  mutate(diabetes = coalesce(diabetes_entry, FALSE) |
           coalesce(diabetes_history, FALSE)) |>
  select(entry_id, diabetes)

count(flags, diabetes)
```

`r sum(flags$diabetes)` entries have diabetes recorded on the entry admission or in
the year before, and `r sum(!flags$diabetes)` do not. Looking back matters:
`r sum(by_period$diabetes_history %in% TRUE & !by_period$diabetes_entry)` of them
have no diabetes code on the entry admission, only on an admission in the year
before.

Reading `NA` as `FALSE` is a study decision: state it in your methods. For the
`r sum(entries$adm_date < as.Date("2022-10-01"))` entries admitted in fiscal
year 2565, part of the year before lies before the first stacked table ([Look
back and follow up](look-back-follow-up.html#windows-and-the-years-you-stacked)),
so their `FALSE` covers less than a year.

A flag records whether a code appears, not how often.

## Several lists at once

One call can flag several conditions. Add hypertension (I10 to I15) and chronic
kidney disease (N18), and count the entry admissions with each:

```{r several}
conditions <- list(
  diabetes = paste0("E", 10:14),
  hypertension = paste0("I", 10:15),
  ckd = "N18"
)

several <- icd_flag(entry_admissions, conditions,
                    id = "entry_id", cols = dx_cols,
                    match = "prefix")
summarise(several, across(-entry_id, sum))
```

Each name became a column. Names must be unique and differ from the ID column;
a condition with no codes, `character(0)`, matches nothing.

## Exact or prefix

`match = "exact"`, the default, matches whole codes; `"prefix"` matches every
code that starts with one on your list. The choice matters because Thai records
often carry a fifth character: F10.3, for example, has F10.30 and F10.31
beneath it. With `"exact"`, a list written only at three or four characters
silently misses them. Flag three codes both ways:

```{r exact-prefix}
e11 <- list(e11 = "E11", e116 = "E116", e119 = "E119")

exact <- icd_flag(entry_admissions, e11, id = "entry_id",
                  cols = dx_cols)
prefix <- icd_flag(entry_admissions, e11, id = "entry_id",
                   cols = dx_cols, match = "prefix")

bind_rows(exact = exact, prefix = prefix, .id = "match") |>
  group_by(match) |>
  summarise(across(starts_with("e11"), sum))
```

No entry admission has the bare three-character E11, so exact E11 finds none.
The five-character E1165 is on `r sum(prefix$e116)` of them: exact E116 misses it
and prefix E116 finds it. E119 finds `r sum(exact$e119)` either way, because no
longer code starts with it here. Use `"prefix"` for lists written at three or
four characters, and `"exact"` when you mean exactly the codes listed.

## Choose the columns

`cols` decides which diagnosis positions count. Every entry admission has
appendicitis as its principal diagnosis, so `pdx` alone finds no diabetes; the
secondary diagnoses alone give `NA` to entries with none:

```{r columns}
icd_flag(entry_admissions, dm, id = "entry_id",
         cols = "pdx", match = "prefix") |>
  count(diabetes)

icd_flag(entry_admissions, dm, id = "entry_id",
         cols = paste0("sdx", 1:20), match = "prefix") |>
  count(diabetes)
```

Choose `cols` for your question: `pdx` alone asks what the admission was for;
every position asks what was recorded during it.

## Codes are cleaned first

Before comparing, thipR cleans every code, on your lists and in the records: it
removes dots, makes letters upper case and trims the spaces around each code.
`thip_filter_icd()` uses the same rules on the database. Across all admissions,
count the records whose first secondary diagnosis is E119, however it is
written, then try a carelessly typed list:

```{r cleaned}
admissions |>
  thip_filter_icd(codes = "E119", cols = "sdx1") |>
  count(sdx1) |>
  arrange(sdx1)

messy <- list(diabetes = c("e11.9", " E11.65 "))
icd_flag(entry_admissions, messy, id = "entry_id",
         cols = dx_cols) |>
  count(diabetes)
```

One record in the example writes its code with a dot, `E11.9`, and the search
still finds it. The careless list matches E119 and E1165 and flags the same
`r sum(on_entry$diabetes)` entry admissions. Before you freeze a list, count
which codes occur, at which lengths and in which positions, as in [Check before
you trust](data-checks.html#the-shape-of-codes).

## A quick look with sdx_index

The notebook platform also gives `sdx_index`, a record's secondary diagnoses
joined into one text ([Meet the THIP data](meet-the-data.html)); in the example,
spaces separate the codes. Searching it with `grepl()` is a fast way to peek at
a few codes. Count the entry admissions that each pattern finds:

```{r quick-look}
sdx_text <- entry_admissions$sdx_index
patterns <- c("E11", "K35", "^E11", "E11.9")
found <- sapply(patterns,
                function(p) sum(grepl(p, sdx_text)))
found
```

`"E11"` works: it finds the same `r found[["E11"]]` entry admissions as
`icd_flag()`. The other patterns show the traps:

- **It leaves out `pdx`.** `"K35"` finds nothing, although every entry
  admission has appendicitis there.
- **Patterns are not codes.** `^` is the start of the whole text, not of each
  code, so `"^E11"` checks only the first code and finds `r found[["^E11"]]`; a
  dot means any character, so `"E11.9"` misses every E119; and case matters.
- **It answers per record.** You still combine each entry's records, the year
  before included, and the `r sum(sdx_text == "")` blank values give `FALSE`,
  not `NA`.

So `grepl()` on `sdx_index` is fine for a quick look at a few codes. For flags
you analyse, use `icd_flag()`: it searches `pdx` too, matches whole codes or
prefixes, cleans the codes, combines records per ID, keeps `NA` apart and takes
several lists at once.

## On the database or in R

`thip_filter_icd()`, from [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html),
matches codes by the same rules but filters records on the database: a query
and one vector of codes go in, and a query of the matching records, unchanged,
comes out. `icd_flag()` answers per ID in R, from collected records and named
lists. It refuses a query rather than collecting it for you, so `collect()`
always marks where records come into R.

## Ranges and wildcards

Neither `thip_filter_icd()` nor `icd_flag()` expands notation. A range written
with a hyphen or a dash, such as `"Q20-Q26"`, the wildcards `%` and `_`,
regular-expression symbols such as `^ $ ? | \` or brackets, and several codes
in one string, separated by commas or spaces, stop with an error. `*`, `+` and
`/` do not: some sources write them as part of a code (dagger and asterisk
codes), so thipR keeps them, after removing dots. So `"E11*"` or `"E11.*"` is
read as the code `E11*`:

```{r literal}
starred <- list(e11_star = "E11*", e11 = "E11")
star <- icd_flag(entry_admissions, starred, id = "entry_id",
                 cols = dx_cols, match = "prefix")
summarise(star, across(-entry_id, sum))
```

`"E11*"` quietly matches nothing: no error, no warning, just `FALSE` for all
`r nrow(star)` entry admissions. For E11 and everything beneath it, write
`"E11"` with `match = "prefix"`, which finds `r sum(star$e11)`. For a range,
write the codes out: `paste0("Q", 20:26)` with `match = "prefix"` covers Q20 to
Q26 and every code beneath them.

## The flags table

`flags`, one row per entry with `entry_id` and `diabetes`, is what the [Worked
example](getting-started.html) uses. That guide builds it in one call: as
`icd_flag()` combines all records with the same ID, it stacks the entry
admissions on `history` and flags them together. Check that both ways agree:

```{r one-call}
one_call <- bind_rows(entry_admissions, history) |>
  icd_flag(dm, id = "entry_id", cols = dx_cols,
           match = "prefix") |>
  mutate(diabetes = coalesce(diabetes, FALSE))

flags |>
  left_join(one_call, by = "entry_id",
            suffix = c("", "_one_call")) |>
  count(diabetes, diabetes_one_call)
```

Every entry gets the same answer both ways, and `r sum(one_call$diabetes)`
entries have diabetes.

## A comorbidity screen

One condition is the simple case. `icd_flag()` pays off when a study screens
many, as a comorbidity screen does. Write the conditions as one declared list,
which reads as a table of definitions and can be kept with your protocol. The
lists below illustrate the shape and are not validated definitions; for a real
study, use and cite a reviewed set, such as a published Charlson or Elixhauser
coding.

```{r comorbidity-list}
comorbidities <- list(
  diabetes = paste0("E", 10:14),
  hypertension = paste0("I", 10:15),
  ihd = paste0("I", 20:25),
  heart_failure = "I50",
  stroke = paste0("I", 60:64),
  copd = "J44",
  ckd = "N18",
  cirrhosis = c("K703", "K746"),
  colorectal_cancer = c("C18", "C19", "C20"),
  dementia = c("F00", "F01", "F02", "F03", "G30")
)
```

One call over each entry's admission and its year of history gives one row per
entry and one column per condition. Read `NA` as `FALSE`, as above, and join
the result onto `entries`:

```{r comorbidity-screen}
screen <- bind_rows(entry_admissions, history) |>
  icd_flag(comorbidities, id = "entry_id",
           cols = dx_cols, match = "prefix") |>
  mutate(across(-entry_id, ~ coalesce(.x, FALSE)))

cohort <- entries |>
  left_join(screen, by = "entry_id")

sapply(select(cohort, diabetes:dementia), sum)
```

`cohort` is one row per entry with its dates and ten `TRUE`/`FALSE` columns,
ready for a table of characteristics or a model. In the example several
conditions are never recorded, and every entry gets `FALSE` for them. For 0/1
columns, add
`mutate(across(diabetes:dementia, as.integer))`. Adding a condition means
adding one line to the list.

The hand-written alternative pastes each record's codes into one text, runs one
`grepl()` per condition and then combines the records of each entry: more code
to read and check, and the traps of [A quick look with
sdx_index](#a-quick-look-with-sdx_index). It is also slower as the list grows:
on 200,000 invented records with 21 code columns and these ten conditions,
`icd_flag()` took about a third of the time and gave the same answers. For one
or two codes, `grepl()` can be as quick.

## In short

- A condition is a named list of reviewed codes. `icd_flag()` combines each
  ID's records, rows and columns, into `TRUE`, `FALSE` or `NA`; it reads no dates.
- An entry with no records gets no row: start from `entries`, left-join, and
  decide what `NA` means. This course reads it as `FALSE`.
- `"exact"` is the default; use `"prefix"` for lists written at three or four
  characters, because Thai records often carry a fifth. Choose the positions in
  `cols` to fit the question.
- Dots, case and surrounding spaces are cleaned. Ranges, `%` and `_` stop with
  an error, but `E11*` is read literally and matches nothing: write the codes
  out and use `"prefix"`.
- For a comorbidity screen, declare all the conditions in one list and flag
  them in one call: one row per entry, ready to join onto `entries`.
- `grepl()` on `sdx_index` is a quick look, not a flag. `thip_filter_icd()`
  filters on the database; `icd_flag()` flags collected records in R.

Next: [Worked example](getting-started.html) joins `flags` to `readmit` and
compares readmission in people with and without diabetes.

DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```
